implementation_notes: Vapor supplies the manager as SessionsMiddleware plus req.session: the middleware creates the vapor_session cookie on first write, SessionDriver implementations (in-memory default, Fluent database, Redis) store the record, and app.sessions.configuration.cookieFactory controls cookie attributes. req.session.destroy() invalidates the driver record and clears the cookie. The classic manager/store split therefore collapses into middleware plus driver; what remains is choosing a persistent driver for production and applying token-based stateless authentication for pure APIs, which Vapor's documentation recommends.
code_sketch:
app.sessions.use(.redis)                        // shared, persistent driver
app.middleware.use(app.sessions.middleware)     // value type: configure before use
app.get("login") { req in
    req.session.data["user"] = id
    return .ok
}
app.get("logout") { req in req.session.destroy(); return .ok }
pitfalls: The in-memory driver does not persist across launches or share between instances; it is a test and development default.
The driver must be selected before the middleware is added, because SessionsMiddleware is a value type copied into the application.
For APIs, stateless token-based authentication avoids the session store entirely; the documentation recommends it over sessions for non-browser clients.
